extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, judges, and intellectual property practitioners (design-patent context)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance from the U.S. Supreme Court on how to interpret 'article of manufacture' and compute damages under 35 U.S.C. §289 in design-patent infringement cases, particularly for multicomponent products (e.g., smartphones).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of 'article of manufacture' under §289
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'article of manufacture' as used in §289 'encompasses both a product sold to a consumer and a component of that product.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court explains that 'article' is 'a particular thing' and 'manufacture' means things made by hand or machine, so a component of a multicomponent product is within the phrase. The fact a component is integrated into a larger product or not sold separately does not exclude it from being an 'article of manufacture.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-step §289 damages framework
rubrics_metrics.description: To arrive at a §289 damages award: (1) identify the 'article of manufacture' to which the infringed design has been applied; (2) calculate the infringer's 'total profit' made on that article of manufacture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'total' is interpreted as 'all' (i.e., the whole profit made from the manufacture or sale of the identified article). The first-step identification of the relevant article is a threshold legal determination; the second-step is an accounting of profits on that article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Components may be the relevant article of manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: In the case of a multicomponent product, the relevant 'article of manufacture' for §289 need not be the end product sold to the consumer and may be only a component of that product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This permits recovery of the infringer's total profit attributable to a component (if that component is the identified article), not necessarily only profits from the end product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of 'sold separately' as required test (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: A component need not have been sold separately to ordinary consumers to qualify as the relevant 'article of manufacture.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit's rule—limiting 'article of manufacture' to components sold separately (i.e., that consumers could purchase the component apart from the whole)—is inconsistent with §289 and therefore rejected. Treat reliance on separate-sale evidence as insufficient on its own to exclude a component.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with §171(a): design patents can cover components
rubrics_metrics.description: §171(a) authorizes 'design[s] for an article of manufacture,' and has long been understood to permit design patents that extend to only a component of a multicomponent product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative and prior court precedent (e.g., Ex parte Adams; Application of Zahn) recognize that designs for individual parts of combined machines/structures may be separately patented; this supports reading §289 to reach components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with §101 interpretation of 'manufacture'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court reads §289's 'article of manufacture' in light of §101 jurisprudence (Diamond v. Chakrabarty), which treats 'manufacture' broadly and includes 'the parts of a machine considered separately from the machine itself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the established broad definition of 'manufacture'—production of articles for use by converting materials into new forms/qualities—to conclude components are encompassed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical Dobson causation principle and the effect of §289
rubrics_metrics.description: Before §289 (Dobson line of cases), plaintiffs had to show profits were 'due to' the design (i.e., attributable to the design). Congress enacted §289 to provide a specific damages remedy allowing recovery of the infringer's 'total profit' on the article to which the design was applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the historical limitation (Dobson v. Hartford Carpet Co.) requiring attribution of profits to the design was the reason Congress enacted the specific statutory remedy in §289; under §289 the focus is on the article to which the design was applied rather than requiring separate proof of causation of profit by the design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court will not adopt a new detailed test absent adequate briefing
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court declined to formulate a comprehensive test for identifying the relevant 'article of manufacture' for step one of §289 in the absence of adequate briefing from the parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the Court held components can be articles of manufacture, litigants and lower courts must develop and brief any operational test (the Court remanded remaining issues to the Federal Circuit). Do not assume a single Supreme Court-defined multi-factor test from this opinion.
